interrogator_dossier:
# Sterling Infrastructure (STRL) — Forensic Dossier

*Prepared for the investment committee. Six consecutive quarters of earnings calls (Q1 2025 through Q1 2026) cross-referenced against the screener's actual financial trajectory. Live price used throughout: $622.60 (NASDAQ, intraday 2026-07-17), down about 38% from the recent high near $1,006 and up roughly 103% year-to-date.*

## 1. NARRATIVE ARC

Sterling is a specialty construction company that has, over these six quarters, transformed itself in front of investors from a diversified "roads, sites and houses" contractor into a data-center site-development and electrical powerhouse. The story did not shift so much as one leg of it caught fire and the others were quietly repositioned around it.

At the start of the window (Q1 2025, call dated 2025-05-06), the pitch was balanced: E-Infrastructure Solutions (large-scale site development — earthmoving, grading, underground utilities for big facilities) growing "over 18%," Transportation growing 9%, and Building Solutions (residential concrete) sliding on housing affordability. Data centers were "the primary growth driver," up "approximately 60%." Backlog was $2.1 billion.

By the most recent call (Q1 2026, dated 2026-05-05), that same E-Infrastructure segment grew **174%** (over 100% organically), data centers were again "the primary growth driver," signed backlog reached **$3.8 billion** (combined $5.2 billion), and the total visibility pool — signed backlog plus unsigned electrical awards plus future-phase site work — approached **$6.5 billion**, "grown by approximately $2.0 billion since year end." The single most important strategic move was the September-2025 close of the CEC Facilities Group acquisition (~$450 million of cash), which bolted mission-critical electrical and mechanical services onto Sterling's site-development base — turning the company into a "site-plus-electrical" one-stop shop for data-center campuses.

Three drivers were *introduced or amplified* across the arc: (1) the data-center/AI-capex wave, which went from "60% growth" to "125%+" (Q3 2025) to revenue "more than doubling"; (2) the CEC electrical integration and modular prefabrication build-out; (3) geographic expansion into Texas and the Rocky Mountains. One driver was *managed down*: Building Solutions (residential), openly described as headwind-bound "throughout 2026," and the low-bid Texas heavy-highway operation, deliberately wound down to redeploy assets into higher-margin E-Infrastructure work.

## 2. CLAIMS vs FINANCIALS (forensic)

Management's narrative is unusually well-corroborated by the hard numbers — this is not a story running ahead of its financials; if anything the financials have run ahead of the story.

| Management claim | The financials | Verdict |
|---|---|---|
| "Bottom-line growth roughly double top-line" (Q2 2025) | Revenue 3-yr CAGR +12.1%, EPS 3-yr CAGR +39.2%; 2024→2025 revenue +17.7% while EPS +13.4% on a GAAP basis but adjusted EPS +53% | Holds — operating leverage is real and large |
| Margins "continue to expand" | Gross margin 23.0% and expanding; net margin 11.7% (roughly double the 3–6% typical of engineering-and-construction peers); adjusted EBITDA margin crossed 20% "for the first time in our history" (2025) | Holds — and the margin is the whole thesis |
| Backlog and visibility "anchor our confidence" | Signed backlog $2.1B (Q1'25) → $3.8B (Q1'26); book-to-burn 2.1x in Q1 2026; visibility pool ~$6.5B | Holds — multi-year visibility is genuine, not hand-waving |
| Balance sheet "in great shape" | Net cash of about $224M at 2026-03-31 (cash $512M vs debt $287M); Altman-Z 9.9 (bankruptcy-remote); Piotroski 7/9 | Holds — pristine; a genuine sum-of-the-parts add-back |
| 2026 guide: revenue $3.7–3.8B, adjusted EPS $18.40–19.05 (+72%) | Q1 2026 already printed revenue +92% and adjusted EPS +120%; the full-year guide was *raised* at Q1 by 36% at the adjusted-EPS midpoint | Holds — and the guide has only gone up |

Where the story is *richer* than the numbers: management frames rising margins as structural ("not at a peak because they will continue to go up," Q1 2026). The financials show margins are 1.89 standard deviations above their own historical peak (per the screener) — an extraordinary reading that says these are, statistically, the best margins this business has ever earned. That is a fact to respect, not a fact to extrapolate indefinitely.

Where the story is *poorer* than the multiple: free cash flow. Trailing-twelve-month free cash flow is $440M, but on the live $622.60 price the shares fetch roughly 43x that — and the annual free-cash-flow line actually declined about 13% year-over-year even as earnings soared, because a fast-growing contractor consumes working capital. The cash generation is strong in absolute terms but does not yet justify a growth-stock multiple on its own.

## 3. TONE & CONFIDENCE TRAJECTORY

**Rising, and unusually so.** The language moves steadily from "off to a great start" (Q1 2025) to "another outstanding quarter" (Q3 2025) to "off to a fantastic start" and "an even better year than we originally anticipated" (Q1 2026). Crucially, confidence rose *with specificity*, not in place of it: each call added harder numbers (backlog figures, book-to-burn ratios, a named $500M+ semiconductor-fab first phase in Q1 2026), which is the opposite of the vaguer-as-they-get-nervous pattern.

The tone is offensive throughout — growth, capacity, "if I had 2,000 more electricians, we could put them to work in a quarter" (Q1 2026). The only defensive notes are honest and narrow: residential is "tough… certainly first half of 2026," and permitting delays "cascade." Management repeatedly volunteers the weak spot (Building Solutions) rather than burying it — a credibility positive.

## 4. GUIDANCE CREDIBILITY

**High.** The screener records a 7-of-7 (100%) earnings-beat rate, and the qualitative record matches: 2025 guidance was raised at Q1, again at Q2, again at Q3, and the full year landed on "fifth consecutive year of adjusted EPS growth over 35%." Then 2026 guidance was raised 36% at the adjusted-EPS midpoint at the very first quarter of the year. There is a mild sandbagging pattern — they set a number they are confident they can beat, then beat it — but it is disciplined rather than promotional, and it has been reliable across the whole window. Reliability: **High.**

## 5. ANALYST PRESSURE POINTS

The recurring analyst worry is exactly the right one: **are these peak margins, and is the growth durable or a data-center bubble?** In Q1 2026 an analyst asked point-blank whether E-Infrastructure margins are "structurally sustainable, or are they peak margins." Management's answer — margins are not at a peak "because they will continue to go up" — is confident but unfalsifiable, and it is the single claim the committee should stress-test hardest.

A second pressure point is the infrastructure-bill cliff: the current federal transportation bill (IIJA) ends September 2026, and analysts probed it repeatedly. Management's answer is credible and consistent (two years of backlog in hand, extensions historically bridge any gap) and Transportation is the smaller, steadier segment, so this is a manageable worry rather than a hidden landmine.

What analysts are *not* pushing on, and should: customer concentration. E-Infrastructure is now over 90% mission-critical (data centers, semiconductor, large manufacturing), which means a handful of hyperscaler and chip customers drive the majority of the growth. No call quantified that concentration.

## 6. RED FLAGS / GREEN FLAGS

🟢 100% beat rate corroborated by consistent guidance raises (Q1 2025 → Q1 2026).
🟢 Net cash of about $224M and Altman-Z of 9.9 — the balance sheet cannot force a bad outcome.
🟢 Margins expanding across every quarter, with adjusted EBITDA margin above 20% for the first time ever (2025).
🟢 Management transparent about the weak segment (residential) rather than obscuring it.
🔴 Margins sit 1.89 standard deviations above the company's own historical peak — statistically extreme, and the whole valuation rests on them holding.
🔴 Revenue and earnings are now overwhelmingly levered to one secular driver (AI/data-center capex); E-Infrastructure is over 90% mission-critical backlog. This is textbook single-factor concentration.
🔴 Open-market insider behaviour is one-sided *selling*: one buy of 8,120 shares against 28 sells totalling 477,026 shares. The grant-inflated "buy ratio" in the raw scan masks this; the real signal is that insiders have been distributing into strength.
🔴 Free cash flow declined about 13% year-over-year even as earnings soared — the growth consumes working capital, and the price is roughly 43x trailing free cash flow.

## 7. HIDDEN SIGNALS

The most telling terminology shift is from "fill-in projects" meaning $3–10 million jobs (Q1 2025) to "our guys call the $40 million to $90 million e-commerce distribution projects fill-in projects" (Q2 2025) — the unit of work has grown 10x in the team's own vocabulary in a single year. Capital allocation tells the same story: buybacks were done at an average of $128.98 in Q1 2025 and, revealingly, only $12 million at an average of **$305.14** in Q1 2026 — management slowed repurchases sharply as the stock ran, which is disciplined but also a quiet signal that they did not see the higher price as a bargain. The CFO transition (Ron Ballschmiede to Nick Grindstaff, mid-2025) was smooth with no change in tone or disclosure quality.

## 8. CAPITAL-ALLOCATION VERDICT (for the director)

**Trajectory: STRENGTHENING.** Every operating metric — revenue growth, margins, backlog, earnings, balance-sheet strength — is accelerating, and management's credibility is corroborated by a perfect beat record. This is a genuinely excellent, well-run franchise.

The single most important thing to weigh before sizing: **this is not the deep-value name the signal implies — it is a high-quality, high-growth, AI-capex-levered cyclical trading at roughly 37x forward earnings after a 38% crash, and even at the lower price it sits well above a disciplined sum-of-the-parts value.** The crash has taken a very expensive stock (~60x at the $1,006 high) down to a still-expensive one; it has not yet created a margin of safety. The load-bearing question is whether data-center construction demand and record margins both persist — a single shared driver on both sides of the thesis.

**Economic moat: narrow, but widening.** The moat type is scale-plus-execution (reputation for finishing mission-critical jobs on schedule, geographic footprint, and now the CEC site-plus-electrical bundle that shortens project cycle time) — real advantages, but a contractor's advantages, with low customer switching costs and project-by-project competition. Return on invested capital of 13.2% is only modestly above the cost of capital, which is the tell that this is a narrow moat rather than a wide one; return on equity of 24% is flattered by operating leverage at the top of a cycle. The trend is genuinely widening (E-Infrastructure operating margins moved from ~23% toward ~28%, and company-wide EBITDA margin crossed 20% for the first time). **Secular threat: manageable, not terminal.** Sterling is a *beneficiary* of the AI build-out, not a victim of a structural decline, so there is no terminal-value impairment story here. The real risk is cyclical — an AI-capex digestion — not secular erosion. The cheapness signal is therefore misleading in a different way than usual: it is not a value trap on a shrinking base, it is an optically-cheap-looking growth name that is in fact still richly priced on any normalized view.

CREDIBILITY_SCORE: 5 | TRAJECTORY: STRENGTHENING | MOAT: NARROW | MOAT_TREND: WIDENING | SECULAR_THREAT: manageable

# Sterling Infrastructure (STRL) — Forensic Dossier

*Prepared for the investment committee. Six consecutive quarters of earnings calls (Q1 2025 through Q1 2026) cross-referenced against the screener's actual financial trajectory. Live price used throughout: $622.60 (NASDAQ, intraday 2026-07-17), down about 38% from the recent high near $1,006 and up roughly 103% year-to-date.*

## 1. NARRATIVE ARC

Sterling is a specialty construction company that has, over these six quarters, transformed itself in front of investors from a diversified "roads, sites and houses" contractor into a data-center site-development and electrical powerhouse. The story did not shift so much as one leg of it caught fire and the others were quietly repositioned around it.

At the start of the window (Q1 2025, call dated 2025-05-06), the pitch was balanced: E-Infrastructure Solutions (large-scale site development — earthmoving, grading, underground utilities for big facilities) growing "over 18%," Transportation growing 9%, and Building Solutions (residential concrete) sliding on housing affordability. Data centers were "the primary growth driver," up "approximately 60%." Backlog was $2.1 billion.

By the most recent call (Q1 2026, dated 2026-05-05), that same E-Infrastructure segment grew **174%** (over 100% organically), data centers were again "the primary growth driver," signed backlog reached **$3.8 billion** (combined $5.2 billion), and the total visibility pool — signed backlog plus unsigned electrical awards plus future-phase site work — approached **$6.5 billion**, "grown by approximately $2.0 billion since year end." The single most important strategic move was the September-2025 close of the CEC Facilities Group acquisition (~$450 million of cash), which bolted mission-critical electrical and mechanical services onto Sterling's site-development base — turning the company into a "site-plus-electrical" one-stop shop for data-center campuses.

Three drivers were *introduced or amplified* across the arc: (1) the data-center/AI-capex wave, which went from "60% growth" to "125%+" (Q3 2025) to revenue "more than doubling"; (2) the CEC electrical integration and modular prefabrication build-out; (3) geographic expansion into Texas and the Rocky Mountains. One driver was *managed down*: Building Solutions (residential), openly described as headwind-bound "throughout 2026," and the low-bid Texas heavy-highway operation, deliberately wound down to redeploy assets into higher-margin E-Infrastructure work.

## 2. CLAIMS vs FINANCIALS (forensic)

Management's narrative is unusually well-corroborated by the hard numbers — this is not a story running ahead of its financials; if anything the financials have run ahead of the story.

| Management claim | The financials | Verdict |
|---|---|---|
| "Bottom-line growth roughly double top-line" (Q2 2025) | Revenue 3-yr CAGR +12.1%, EPS 3-yr CAGR +39.2%; 2024→2025 revenue +17.7% while EPS +13.4% on a GAAP basis but adjusted EPS +53% | Holds — operating leverage is real and large |
| Margins "continue to expand" | Gross margin 23.0% and expanding; net margin 11.7% (roughly double the 3–6% typical of engineering-and-construction peers); adjusted EBITDA margin crossed 20% "for the first time in our history" (2025) | Holds — and the margin is the whole thesis |
| Backlog and visibility "anchor our confidence" | Signed backlog $2.1B (Q1'25) → $3.8B (Q1'26); book-to-burn 2.1x in Q1 2026; visibility pool ~$6.5B | Holds — multi-year visibility is genuine, not hand-waving |
| Balance sheet "in great shape" | Net cash of about $224M at 2026-03-31 (cash $512M vs debt $287M); Altman-Z 9.9 (bankruptcy-remote); Piotroski 7/9 | Holds — pristine; a genuine sum-of-the-parts add-back |
| 2026 guide: revenue $3.7–3.8B, adjusted EPS $18.40–19.05 (+72%) | Q1 2026 already printed revenue +92% and adjusted EPS +120%; the full-year guide was *raised* at Q1 by 36% at the adjusted-EPS midpoint | Holds — and the guide has only gone up |

Where the story is *richer* than the numbers: management frames rising margins as structural ("not at a peak because they will continue to go up," Q1 2026). The financials show margins are 1.89 standard deviations above their own historical peak (per the screener) — an extraordinary reading that says these are, statistically, the best margins this business has ever earned. That is a fact to respect, not a fact to extrapolate indefinitely.

Where the story is *poorer* than the multiple: free cash flow. Trailing-twelve-month free cash flow is $440M, but on the live $622.60 price the shares fetch roughly 43x that — and the annual free-cash-flow line actually declined about 13% year-over-year even as earnings soared, because a fast-growing contractor consumes working capital. The cash generation is strong in absolute terms but does not yet justify a growth-stock multiple on its own.

## 3. TONE & CONFIDENCE TRAJECTORY

**Rising, and unusually so.** The language moves steadily from "off to a great start" (Q1 2025) to "another outstanding quarter" (Q3 2025) to "off to a fantastic start" and "an even better year than we originally anticipated" (Q1 2026). Crucially, confidence rose *with specificity*, not in place of it: each call added harder numbers (backlog figures, book-to-burn ratios, a named $500M+ semiconductor-fab first phase in Q1 2026), which is the opposite of the vaguer-as-they-get-nervous pattern.

The tone is offensive throughout — growth, capacity, "if I had 2,000 more electricians, we could put them to work in a quarter" (Q1 2026). The only defensive notes are honest and narrow: residential is "tough… certainly first half of 2026," and permitting delays "cascade." Management repeatedly volunteers the weak spot (Building Solutions) rather than burying it — a credibility positive.

## 4. GUIDANCE CREDIBILITY

**High.** The screener records a 7-of-7 (100%) earnings-beat rate, and the qualitative record matches: 2025 guidance was raised at Q1, again at Q2, again at Q3, and the full year landed on "fifth consecutive year of adjusted EPS growth over 35%." Then 2026 guidance was raised 36% at the adjusted-EPS midpoint at the very first quarter of the year. There is a mild sandbagging pattern — they set a number they are confident they can beat, then beat it — but it is disciplined rather than promotional, and it has been reliable across the whole window. Reliability: **High.**

## 5. ANALYST PRESSURE POINTS

The recurring analyst worry is exactly the right one: **are these peak margins, and is the growth durable or a data-center bubble?** In Q1 2026 an analyst asked point-blank whether E-Infrastructure margins are "structurally sustainable, or are they peak margins." Management's answer — margins are not at a peak "because they will continue to go up" — is confident but unfalsifiable, and it is the single claim the committee should stress-test hardest.

A second pressure point is the infrastructure-bill cliff: the current federal transportation bill (IIJA) ends September 2026, and analysts probed it repeatedly. Management's answer is credible and consistent (two years of backlog in hand, extensions historically bridge any gap) and Transportation is the smaller, steadier segment, so this is a manageable worry rather than a hidden landmine.

What analysts are *not* pushing on, and should: customer concentration. E-Infrastructure is now over 90% mission-critical (data centers, semiconductor, large manufacturing), which means a handful of hyperscaler and chip customers drive the majority of the growth. No call quantified that concentration.

## 6. RED FLAGS / GREEN FLAGS

🟢 100% beat rate corroborated by consistent guidance raises (Q1 2025 → Q1 2026).
🟢 Net cash of about $224M and Altman-Z of 9.9 — the balance sheet cannot force a bad outcome.
🟢 Margins expanding across every quarter, with adjusted EBITDA margin above 20% for the first time ever (2025).
🟢 Management transparent about the weak segment (residential) rather than obscuring it.
🔴 Margins sit 1.89 standard deviations above the company's own historical peak — statistically extreme, and the whole valuation rests on them holding.
🔴 Revenue and earnings are now overwhelmingly levered to one secular driver (AI/data-center capex); E-Infrastructure is over 90% mission-critical backlog. This is textbook single-factor concentration.
🔴 Open-market insider behaviour is one-sided *selling*: one buy of 8,120 shares against 28 sells totalling 477,026 shares. The grant-inflated "buy ratio" in the raw scan masks this; the real signal is that insiders have been distributing into strength.
🔴 Free cash flow declined about 13% year-over-year even as earnings soared — the growth consumes working capital, and the price is roughly 43x trailing free cash flow.

## 7. HIDDEN SIGNALS

The most telling terminology shift is from "fill-in projects" meaning $3–10 million jobs (Q1 2025) to "our guys call the $40 million to $90 million e-commerce distribution projects fill-in projects" (Q2 2025) — the unit of work has grown 10x in the team's own vocabulary in a single year. Capital allocation tells the same story: buybacks were done at an average of $128.98 in Q1 2025 and, revealingly, only $12 million at an average of **$305.14** in Q1 2026 — management slowed repurchases sharply as the stock ran, which is disciplined but also a quiet signal that they did not see the higher price as a bargain. The CFO transition (Ron Ballschmiede to Nick Grindstaff, mid-2025) was smooth with no change in tone or disclosure quality.

## 8. CAPITAL-ALLOCATION VERDICT (for the director)

**Trajectory: STRENGTHENING.** Every operating metric — revenue growth, margins, backlog, earnings, balance-sheet strength — is accelerating, and management's credibility is corroborated by a perfect beat record. This is a genuinely excellent, well-run franchise.

The single most important thing to weigh before sizing: **this is not the deep-value name the signal implies — it is a high-quality, high-growth, AI-capex-levered cyclical trading at roughly 37x forward earnings after a 38% crash, and even at the lower price it sits well above a disciplined sum-of-the-parts value.** The crash has taken a very expensive stock (~60x at the $1,006 high) down to a still-expensive one; it has not yet created a margin of safety. The load-bearing question is whether data-center construction demand and record margins both persist — a single shared driver on both sides of the thesis.

**Economic moat: narrow, but widening.** The moat type is scale-plus-execution (reputation for finishing mission-critical jobs on schedule, geographic footprint, and now the CEC site-plus-electrical bundle that shortens project cycle time) — real advantages, but a contractor's advantages, with low customer switching costs and project-by-project competition. Return on invested capital of 13.2% is only modestly above the cost of capital, which is the tell that this is a narrow moat rather than a wide one; return on equity of 24% is flattered by operating leverage at the top of a cycle. The trend is genuinely widening (E-Infrastructure operating margins moved from ~23% toward ~28%, and company-wide EBITDA margin crossed 20% for the first time). **Secular threat: manageable, not terminal.** Sterling is a *beneficiary* of the AI build-out, not a victim of a structural decline, so there is no terminal-value impairment story here. The real risk is cyclical — an AI-capex digestion — not secular erosion. The cheapness signal is therefore misleading in a different way than usual: it is not a value trap on a shrinking base, it is an optically-cheap-looking growth name that is in fact still richly priced on any normalized view.

**High.** The screener records a 7-of-7 (100%) earnings-beat rate, and the qualitative record matches: 2025 guidance was raised at Q1, again at Q2, again at Q3, and the full year landed on "fifth consecutive year of adjusted EPS growth over 35%." Then 2026 guidance was raised 36% at the adjusted-EPS midpoint at the very first quarter of the year. There is a mild sandbagging pattern — they set a number they are confident they can beat, then beat it — but it is disciplined rather than promotional, and it has been reliable across the whole window. Reliability: **High.**

## 5. ANALYST PRESSURE POINTS

The recurring analyst worry is exactly the right one: **are these peak margins, and is the growth durable or a data-center bubble?** In Q1 2026 an analyst asked point-blank whether E-Infrastructure margins are "structurally sustainable, or are they peak margins." Management's answer — margins are not at a peak "because they will continue to go up" — is confident but unfalsifiable, and it is the single claim the committee should stress-test hardest.

A second pressure point is the infrastructure-bill cliff: the current federal transportation bill (IIJA) ends September 2026, and analysts probed it repeatedly. Management's answer is credible and consistent (two years of backlog in hand, extensions historically bridge any gap) and Transportation is the smaller, steadier segment, so this is a manageable worry rather than a hidden landmine.

What analysts are *not* pushing on, and should: customer concentration. E-Infrastructure is now over 90% mission-critical (data centers, semiconductor, large manufacturing), which means a handful of hyperscaler and chip customers drive the majority of the growth. No call quantified that concentration.

## 7. HIDDEN SIGNALS

The most telling terminology shift is from "fill-in projects" meaning $3–10 million jobs (Q1 2025) to "our guys call the $40 million to $90 million e-commerce distribution projects fill-in projects" (Q2 2025) — the unit of work has grown 10x in the team's own vocabulary in a single year. Capital allocation tells the same story: buybacks were done at an average of $128.98 in Q1 2025 and, revealingly, only $12 million at an average of **$305.14** in Q1 2026 — management slowed repurchases sharply as the stock ran, which is disciplined but also a quiet signal that they did not see the higher price as a bargain. The CFO transition (Ron Ballschmiede to Nick Grindstaff, mid-2025) was smooth with no change in tone or disclosure quality.

## 8. CAPITAL-ALLOCATION VERDICT (for the director)

**Trajectory: STRENGTHENING.** Every operating metric — revenue growth, margins, backlog, earnings, balance-sheet strength — is accelerating, and management's credibility is corroborated by a perfect beat record. This is a genuinely excellent, well-run franchise.

The single most important thing to weigh before sizing: **this is not the deep-value name the signal implies — it is a high-quality, high-growth, AI-capex-levered cyclical trading at roughly 37x forward earnings after a 38% crash, and even at the lower price it sits well above a disciplined sum-of-the-parts value.** The crash has taken a very expensive stock (~60x at the $1,006 high) down to a still-expensive one; it has not yet created a margin of safety. The load-bearing question is whether data-center construction demand and record margins both persist — a single shared driver on both sides of the thesis.

**Economic moat: narrow, but widening.** The moat type is scale-plus-execution (reputation for finishing mission-critical jobs on schedule, geographic footprint, and now the CEC site-plus-electrical bundle that shortens project cycle time) — real advantages, but a contractor's advantages, with low customer switching costs and project-by-project competition. Return on invested capital of 13.2% is only modestly above the cost of capital, which is the tell that this is a narrow moat rather than a wide one; return on equity of 24% is flattered by operating leverage at the top of a cycle. The trend is genuinely widening (E-Infrastructure operating margins moved from ~23% toward ~28%, and company-wide EBITDA margin crossed 20% for the first time). **Secular threat: manageable, not terminal.** Sterling is a *beneficiary* of the AI build-out, not a victim of a structural decline, so there is no terminal-value impairment story here. The real risk is cyclical — an AI-capex digestion — not secular erosion. The cheapness signal is therefore misleading in a different way than usual: it is not a value trap on a shrinking base, it is an optically-cheap-looking growth name that is in fact still richly priced on any normalized view.
